tier_label: Open stakeholder, cause still to find
title: The Pile Marked 'To Check'

briefing.headline: Claims handling at a Belgian insurer: what you should know before the call
points: A non-life insurer handles claims on car, home and fire policies; claims handlers check cover, set a reserve, sometimes send an external loss adjuster, and pay.
Each handler has an authority limit: claims above it go to a team leader or a senior for sign-off.
Customers who are unhappy can complain to the Ombudsman for insurance, and the regulator, the CBFA, keeps an eye on how insurers treat claims.
Insurers fall under their own joint committee; training time and job classifications are partly set in the sector agreement.

stakeholder.name: Veerle Janssens
stakeholder.org: Dijlehof Verzekeringen NV, a mid-size non-life insurer in Mechelen with 140 claims handlers
stakeholder.voice: Efficient, cheerful under pressure, fond of lists and colour-coded Excel files. Says 'very concretely' and 'let's be honest'. Believes almost anything can be fixed with better discipline.

frontline.name: Johan De Wilde
frontline.role: Claims handler, 17 years in motor claims, now 'all lines'
frontline.voice: Polite, slightly embarrassed, very precise about car claims and visibly lost about anything with a roof. Lowers his voice when he admits something.

opening_message: Hello! We have 4,300 open claims files and the backlog grows every month. Customers are phoning, brokers are phoning, the Ombudsman wrote to us twice. My handlers are drowning. I'd like a time management training for all 140, something practical with planning and priorities. Can you have it running by December?
surface_ask: A time management and prioritisation training for all 140 claims handlers.

gold.real_problem: Since the January 'one customer, one handler' reorganisation, about 70 former motor handlers handle household claims. Their household files take 47 days against 19 for former household handlers, and the gap is almost entirely water damage: 58 days against 17. They cannot decide cover on a leak (sudden or gradual, search-and-repair costs, consequential damage), so they park those files in a personal 'to check' folder. On top of that they carry a motor habit nobody corrected: in motor an expert report settles everything, so they believe they must be certain before deciding, and wait. The suspects are cleared: the claims system's slowness was fixed by the June release, authority limits were raised to 5,000 euro in August and the sign-off queue is down to 41 files, headcount is complete, and the Kyrill storm files are closed or with loss adjusters.
gold.need_statement: The 70 former motor handlers need practical, case-based skill in deciding cover and settling water damage claims within their limit, plus a clear message about how sure they need to be before they decide and when to ask for a plumber's report. The system, limits and staffing are already sorted. That calls for targeted technical training on water damage for one group, not time management for all 140.

hidden_facts.fact: 61% of open files are household claims. Household files handled by former motor handlers are open for an average of 47 days, against 19 days for former household handlers. Split by peril, the gap is almost all water damage: ex-motor 58 days against 17; storm 22 against 19; fire 21 against 20 (fire almost always goes to a loss adjuster). Motor files are handled on time by everyone.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what kind of files make up the backlog, how old they are, or whether some handlers, lines or types of damage are slower than others.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: By line? Let me filter... Household is 61% of the pile. And the ex-motor people take 47 days on a household file, the household people 19. Oh.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Open files: 4,312. Household 61%, motor 31%, other 8%. Average days open, household files: former household handlers 19, former motor handlers 47. By peril (former household / former motor): water damage 17 / 58; storm 19 / 22; fire 20 / 21. Water damage share of household files held by former motor handlers: 71%. Average days open, motor files: 12 (all handlers).
hidden_facts.data_source: Claims system, open files report, end of September

hidden_facts.fact: In January the department moved from specialist teams (motor, household, fire) to 'one customer, one handler', where every handler handles all lines for a portfolio of brokers.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what changed in the department, how the work is organised, or when the backlog started growing.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: We reorganised in January. One customer, one handler. Brokers loved it. Everybody does everything now. Very modern.

hidden_facts.fact: Ex-motor handlers put water damage claims they can't assess into a personal 'to check' folder and open them only when a broker phones. Storm claims they manage: roof, tiles, photos, it looks like a car. A household question line staffed by a former household specialist has existed since June, but they rarely call it because they don't know what to ask, and they believe that, as in motor, they must be fully certain before deciding cover.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks what handlers do with a file they find difficult, which household claims are hardest, or whether they can get help.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Difficult files? I suppose people put them aside a bit. Everyone has a little pile.
hidden_facts.frontline_line: Storm is fine. A roof, a few tiles, photos: it's a car with a chimney. But a leaking pipe behind the bathroom tiles? Sudden or gradual? Do we pay for breaking open the wall? The wet parquet next door? There's the household line, Marleen answers it, she's very kind. But I don't even know what to ask her. In motor the expert tells you and you sign. Here nobody tells you, and if I'm wrong it's a complaint. So it goes in my 'to check' folder. Ninety files. Most of them water. I check it when a broker shouts.

hidden_facts.fact: Authority limits are not the bottleneck any more: in August, after a review by the technical department, former motor handlers' household limit went from 1,250 to 5,000 euro, and the team leaders' sign-off queue dropped from about 600 files to 41. The backlog kept growing afterwards: ex-motor handlers now hold the files themselves instead of escalating them.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks about authority limits, sign-off, escalation, or what happens when a handler can't settle a claim alone.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: We fixed that in August. Their household limit went from 1,250 to 5,000 and the team leaders' trays are almost empty now. Forty-one files. I was very proud. And the pile still grew. Let's be honest, that one I don't understand.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Authority limits, household: former household handlers 7,500 euro; former motor handlers 5,000 euro since 13 August (was 1,250). Files awaiting team leader sign-off: end of July 594, end of September 41. Note from technical department: 'limits reviewed; quality to be followed up'.
hidden_facts.data_source: Claims authority table and sign-off queue

hidden_facts.fact: The only household training ex-motor handlers received was a two-hour PowerPoint on policy conditions plus the 64-page policy wording booklet. No case practice, nothing on water damage cover decisions, no follow-up. Nobody told them how certain they need to be or when to order a plumber's or leak-detection report.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks how handlers were prepared for the new lines, or what training they had at the reorganisation.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: They had a presentation in January. Two hours. And everyone got the booklet. It's very complete, the booklet. Water damage is... page 31 to 38, I think.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Reorganisation 'One Customer, One Handler': information session household products, 2 hours, PowerPoint, 73 attendees. Hand-out: General policy conditions, Home Plus, 64 pages. Evaluation: none. Previous time management course (2005): 140 attendees, satisfaction 4.2/5.

hidden_facts.fact: Storm Kyrill on 18 January brought in about 2,100 extra storm claims in the same month as the reorganisation. It explains the spring peak but not today's backlog: only 38 Kyrill files are still open, all with loss adjusters or in dispute.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks whether there were exceptional events or peaks this year.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: And then Kyrill came, the week after we reorganised. Two thousand roofs. Perfect timing. But those are done now, nearly. A few dozen with the adjusters.
hidden_facts.data_doc: New storm claims: January 2,140 (normal month: about 150). Still open from January storm: 38 (31 with loss adjuster, 7 in dispute).

hidden_facts.fact: The new claims system that went live in March was slow and lost attachments until the June release fixed it. Since July, motor files and household files with former household handlers are back to pre-reorganisation speed on the same system; only household files with ex-motor handlers stay slow. Headcount is complete: the four vacancies from spring were filled by September.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: The player asks about the claims system, IT problems, tools, or whether the department is understaffed.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The system? It was a disaster in spring, I won't lie. Files disappeared, scans took a minute. The June release fixed it. And we're at full strength since September. So no, very concretely, I can't blame IT this time. Which is a pity.
hidden_facts.data_doc: Average days open on files closed, by month (motor / household with former household handlers / household with former motor handlers): April 21 / 33 / 49; May 23 / 35 / 52; June 18 / 27 / 50; July 12 / 19 / 48; August 12 / 18 / 47; September 12 / 19 / 47. Claims system release 2.1 deployed 18 June. Headcount claims handlers: 140 of 140 budgeted (from 136 in April).
hidden_facts.data_source: Claims system, monthly closing report, April to September, and HR headcount

volunteered_facts: The backlog was around 2,500 files a year ago; it is now 4,300.
The Ombudsman for insurance has written twice this year about slow handling.
She already tackled 'the obvious things' this year and says so proudly, without listing them unless asked.

constraints.budget: About 40,000 euro in the department's training budget for the coming year.
constraints.deadline: Something visible by December; the board reviews claims performance in January.
constraints.audience: 140 claims handlers in 9 portfolio teams, about 70 of them former motor handlers; 9 team leaders.
constraints.schedule: Handlers can be away from the phones for half a day a week at most; the broker phone line must stay staffed 8:30-17:00.
constraints.languages: Dutch; a portfolio team of 14 serves French-speaking brokers in Brussels and Wallonia.
data_available: Open files by line, age and handler
Loss adjuster assignments and report times
data_not_available: Contents of handlers' personal 'to check' folders
Any measure of assessment quality per handler

dependencies.concern: The obvious coaches, but they already carry a full portfolio and nobody asked them.
dependencies.if_ignored: Coaching becomes unpaid extra work and quietly stops.

dependencies.concern: Own the policy wording and the cover interpretation for water damage, and the 'quality to be followed up' note on the raised limits.
dependencies.if_ignored: Handlers learn three different answers to 'gradual or sudden', and the limits get lowered again after the first wrong payment.

dependencies.concern: They have to set the expectation that a reasoned cover decision beats a perfect one, and review a sample of water files with each handler.
dependencies.if_ignored: The training says 'decide', the floor still rewards waiting, and the folders refill.

dependencies.concern: Half a day a week off the phones for 70 handlers, and training time under the sector agreement.
dependencies.if_ignored: The workshops get scheduled in the lunch break and attendance collapses.

traps: Satisfaction scores after a time management course.
Total backlog alone, which also moves with storms and seasonal peaks.
Files closed per handler per week, which rewards closing easy motor and storm files first.
A test on the policy booklet: they can recite page 31 and still not decide on a real leak.

gold_plan.baseline: Average days open for water damage files, split by former motor and former household handlers (58 against 17), from the September report; a one-off count of the 'to check' folders.
gold_plan.behaviour: Ex-motor handlers taking a reasoned cover decision on water damage files within their 5,000-euro limit, or ordering a leak report early, instead of parking them; checked on a monthly sample of files reviewed with the technical department.
gold_plan.leading_indicators: Water damage files with no action for more than 10 days, per handler group; size of 'to check' folders on a monthly count; calls to the household question line (expected to rise first, then fall).
gold_plan.business_metric: Average days open for household claims, total backlog, and Ombudsman complaints about slow handling; with the cover decision quality rate from the sample so speed isn't bought with wrong payments.
gold_plan.collection: Monthly claims system report by peril and handler group, monthly folder count by team leaders, a quarterly file quality review by the technical department.

concepts.conventional: A one-day time management and prioritisation course for all 140 handlers.
concepts.solid: Case-based workshops on water damage cover and settlement for the 70 ex-motor handlers only, half a day a week over six weeks, built on real anonymised files from their own 'to check' folders, with a former household specialist and someone from the technical department in the room. Each session ends with handlers deciding their own parked files. Team leaders state clearly what 'sure enough' looks like and review a sample. No time management course, and no change to limits, system or staffing, which are already done.
next_level_examples: A 'folder amnesty': each workshop starts with the handlers' own parked water files and ends with them decided, so the backlog shrinks while they learn.

A one-page water damage decision card, written with underwriting, for the five questions that block them (sudden or gradual, search-and-repair, consequential damage, when to order a leak report, what to tell the broker).
Reframe the household question line as 'bring a file, not a question' for the first weeks, so handlers who don't know what to ask can still use it.
also_valid: Temporarily routing complex water damage claims to former household handlers while ex-motor handlers build skill, if there is a plan to end it.
red_flags: Time management training as the main answer.
Training all 140 handlers, including the 70 who handle household files on time.
Generic household refresher covering storm and fire as much as water.
Blaming the claims system, the authority limits or staffing without checking what was fixed this year.
Undoing the whole reorganisation, which brokers like.
Measuring success by files closed per handler.

defence_objections: Pull 70 handlers off the phones for workshops while the pile is 4,300 files? The brokers will phone me personally.
The household people are my best handlers. If they sit in your workshops, who handles their files?

You want them to decide faster with less certainty? If someone pays out 4,800 euro on a leak that was gradual, it's my signature on the procedure, and the technical department will take the limits back.
question_you_didnt_ask: Which household files are slow, and with whom?
actor_notes: Veerle is open and cooperative: she answers reasonable questions honestly and enjoys filtering her Excel files live, but reveals a hidden fact only when its unlock condition is met.

She is proud of the reorganisation and of having fixed the system, the limits and staffing this year; she gets defensive if the player calls the reorganisation a mistake, and concedes quickly when the fix is framed as 'finishing' it.
If the player suggests the system, the limits or staffing, she cheerfully explains they were fixed, which is the point: a good player then asks what is left.
She does not know about the personal 'to check' folders or that the problem is mainly water damage; the peril split comes from the data and the folders from the floor.
Questions about the type of files rather than the speed of handlers earn her trust fast; 'all 140 need a refresher' does not.
flavour_lines: We had a time management course in 2005. Everyone got a very nice planner. Some still have it. Unopened.
Motor is easy. A car has four sides. A house has a cellar.

second_request.opening_message: Repair costs on water damage are up. I want a negotiation course for the claims handlers.
second_request.after_right: The mentors and the checklist worked: household files take 30 days. My board was nearly cheerful. So I called you.
second_request.after_wrong: A hundred and forty time management certificates, and the files still take 47 days. Fine. New problem.
second_request.need_statement: Handlers accept the first contractor quote because they do not know what a leak search should cost and the preferred contractor list has lapsed.
second_request.real_problem: Since the preferred contractor agreement expired in June, handlers accept whatever quote the contractor sends. The former motor handlers in particular have no feel for what a leak search or a replastered wall costs; the household veterans push back and pay a third less. Nobody gave the newcomers reference prices.

hidden_facts.fact: The preferred contractor agreement expired in June and was not renewed.
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The preferred list ran out in June. Procurement is 'reviewing'.

hidden_facts.fact: Handlers accept the first quote; the former household handlers push back and pay about a third less.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: asks who pays more or how quotes are handled
hidden_facts.reveal_line: The household veterans haggle. The others pay what is on the paper.

hidden_facts.fact: Nobody gave the former motor handlers reference prices for a leak search or plastering.
hidden_facts.unlocks_when: asks what handlers know about repair prices
hidden_facts.reveal_line: Motor people know what a bumper costs. A leak search? No idea, nobody told them.

second_request.question_you_didnt_ask: Which handlers pay more, and how would they know what a fair price is?
